source.title: LLM Interpretability with Identifiable Temporal-Instantaneous Representation
source.authors: Xiang-Chen Song; Jia-Qi Sun; Zi-Jian Li; Yu-Jian Zheng; Kun Zhang

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and figures are flattened or garbled in the text extraction, but the relevant prose is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The authors specifically argue that SAE features lack theoretical uniqueness guarantees and may be arbitrary or unstable, qualifying the claim that SAE features are canonical units. The paper does not test superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper uses SAE-derived features and evaluates its proposed causal representation method, but does not measure feature overlap, near-orthogonality, capacity competition, or whether SAE features are complete and stable in practice. The sole included row records the authors’ explicit theoretical argument about SAE uniqueness; benchmark and relation-recovery outcomes do not directly measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper builds a temporal causal extension of sparse autoencoders and reports only its own method's performance (synthetic recovery, relation-recovery scores, SAEBench metrics, case studies). It assumes linear, sparse latent concepts in LLM activations. It never measures superposition, polysemanticity, or whether standard SAE features are complete, stable or canonical. The SAE-uniqueness remark in the Introduction is a one-sentence motivation citing other work [54]. It is not the study's own result, nor a specific argument developed against V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that their linear temporal causal representation framework jointly models time-delayed and instantaneous concept relations, with identifiability guarantees under stated assumptions. They report that it scales to LLM-sized dimensions where existing CRL methods fail, and that it recovers interpretable relations in Pythia-160m (and Gemma-2-2B) activations while matching standard SAEs on SAEBench.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce or apply the Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports sensitivity of its own method to feature dimensionality, temporal lag, and regularization settings; these are not shown to change any superposition-related outcome.
record.problems: The real-activation analysis centers on pythia-160m-deduped, and the paper notes limitations of its linear approximation and first-order temporal formulation. Its SAE uniqueness critique is theoretical rather than an empirical test of feature canonicality.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were retained: the synthetic recovery, relation-recovery, SAEBench, absorption, and steering-vector results evaluate the proposed method or its general interpretability performance, not the claim versions’ superposition geometry or SAE feature canonicality.

untested.parts: No toy models and no superposition geometry, sparsity transition or near-orthogonality.
No test of capacity competition or polysemantic neurons.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.

Assumes LLM activations are linear mixtures of sparse concepts and trains dictionaries on them. It does not test whether features are spread across neurons or compare against a non-sparse alternative.

Stability, completeness and canonicality of standard SAE features are not measured. The only uniqueness discussion is a cited motivation. The theorems concern the authors' own model's identifiability under assumptions A1–A6.
No test of one-dimensional versus multi-dimensional features. Engels et al. is only cited.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T5/tests classification over-reads a motivational sentence. Table 11 reports absorption fractions and mean split features (~1.0–1.3) for the authors' own dictionaries. These describe their method's outputs, not standard SAE units, and no seed-to-seed stability comparison is reported. They could at most be weak context for V5, not a test of it.

versions.untested_parts: No test of superposition, overlapping directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry.
No test of capacity competition, dedicated dimensions, or polysemantic neurons.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
The paper analyzes interpretable features and relations in LLM activations, but does not test whether features are spread across neurons or whether an SAE recovers such features.
The paper argues that SAE feature uniqueness is not theoretically guaranteed, but does not empirically test completeness, stability, or canonicality of SAE features.
No test of whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: sparse autoencoders (SAEs)
rows.operation_detail: The authors state that SAEs lack theoretical guarantees that recovered features are unique, and that features could be arbitrary or unstable transformations.
rows.value: The authors state that SAEs offer no theoretical guarantee of feature uniqueness; recovered features may be arbitrary or unstable transformations.
rows.note: This is an author argument about lack of guarantees, not empirical evidence that SAE features are noncanonical in a particular model.
rows.check: This is not a result. It is a motivational sentence in the Introduction that cites prior work ([54]) for SAEs lacking uniqueness guarantees. The study gives no evidence on SAE feature stability or canonicality, so the row should be dropped or treated as a cited claim.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
